impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's six-year statute of limitations for claims against the government is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. This eliminates a tolling mechanism that plaintiffs previously relied on in government contract and takings class actions.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government and government-sponsored enterprises benefit from stronger statute-of-limitations defenses, as class action filings will no longer toll the limitations period for individual opt-out or follow-on claims in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors with claims against the government (including takings and breach of contract claims) face significantly shortened windows to file individual suits, as pending class actions will not toll their limitations period under § 2501.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies requires the same full-scope analysis applied to composition claims under Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment claims covering all humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for headache treatment. Judge Dyk's dissent argued the panel created confusion about enablement standards for method claims and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation. The decision has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent scope and biologics competition.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the pharmaceutical and biologics space benefit from a more permissive enablement standard for method-of-treatment claims, allowing broader genus claims to survive validity challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on methods of treatment, potentially limiting the ability to develop and market competing biologic therapies, particularly antibody-based drugs.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—under which a reference patent qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2) based on its provisional application's filing date without requiring a Dynamic Drinkware written description analysis—is correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating Dental Monitoring's patent on dental arch image analysis using deep learning. The court addressed the critical question of when a reference patent can claim an earlier provisional application filing date for prior art purposes under the AIA, specifically whether the Dynamic Drinkware written description requirement applies. This decision directly impacts how prior art dates are determined in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potential narrowing of the circumstances under which reference patents can claim earlier provisional filing dates as prior art, making it harder for IPR petitioners to establish invalidity using references with questionable provisional support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR proceedings to challenge competitor patents may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status of reference patents, potentially increasing the cost and uncertainty of patent challenges.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding the district court improperly excluded Versata's damages expert testimony. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury award. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. This case provides important guidance on trade secret damages methodology and the Daubert standard for expert testimony in software trade secret disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret holders benefit from a more permissive approach to damages models, and the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award affirms that licensing agreements will be enforced as written.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation liability, with potentially larger damages exposure as courts allow a broader range of damages methodologies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government must defer to terms in a pre-existing license agreement, and whether the trial court erred in its application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessment of non-compensatory damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to assess copyright damages via a hypothetical negotiation rather than deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement but vacated the damages award in part. The court held the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and erred by assessing non-compensatory damages against the government for unauthorized copying of TETRA® software used by DOD and DVA. This decision provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government procurement contexts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies benefit from the confirmation that hypothetical negotiation is a valid damages framework even when a license agreement exists, potentially yielding higher damages than strict license terms.
impacts.negativeImplications: Software licensors face limitations on recoverable damages against the government, as non-compensatory damages are impermissible and the 'book of wisdom' doctrine has defined boundaries that may reduce overall awards.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents sufficient to constitute a de facto assignment, allowing the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of TexasLDPC's patent infringement suit against Broadcom, holding that the exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights and thus constituted a de facto assignment. The court also held that TexasLDPC had not ceased its business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement. This decision clarifies the standing requirements for exclusive licensees in patent litigation and the circumstances under which a license agreement amounts to an assignment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent monetization entities benefit from clearer guidance that enforcement-focused business models do not terminate license agreements, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on challenging licensee standing, as courts will more readily find that comprehensive exclusive licenses convey all substantial rights.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents related to non-uniform constellation communication technology, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to communications technology patents, distinguishing between claims that recite abstract mathematical relationships and those that claim specific technological implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for claims directed to specific technological implementations of mathematical concepts, and the affirmance of a damages award validates expert methodologies in standards-essential patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communications standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the partial vacatur on eligibility introduces uncertainty about the scope of patent protection for constellation design innovations.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality questions in design patent claim construction should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent infringement case, with significant disagreement among the judges. The concurrence defended the Egyptian Goddess framework, while the dissent (joined by four judges) argued the framework has improperly shifted focus to dissimilarity, enabling district courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without proper examination of prior art, and that functionality questions should go to the jury. The deep split signals potential instability in design patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the current framework's tendency to allow resolution of design patent disputes at summary judgment based on visual differences, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that four judges believe improperly favors finding non-infringement, and the near-miss en banc vote signals future instability that creates uncertainty for businesses relying on design patent protection.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether such a contract interpretation question must be resolved by the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit transferred T-Mobile's appeal to the Fifth Circuit, holding it lacked jurisdiction because the dispute over whether T-Mobile owed an additional payment under a patent settlement agreement turned on contract interpretation under state law, not a substantial question of patent law. This decision clarifies the boundaries of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over post-settlement patent-related disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that disputes over contract terms will be resolved by regional circuits applying state contract law, providing more predictable interpretation standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement disputes face potential forum uncertainty and additional costs, as jurisdictional questions may need to be litigated before the merits can be reached.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims of a communications apparatus patent reciting transmission of signals 'over air' are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court found the claims indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of invalidity against Satius's patent claims asserted against Samsung, but on alternative grounds. While reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling, the court held the claims invalid for lack of enablement. The decision demonstrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on grounds not relied upon by the district court, providing an important precedent on the interplay between indefiniteness and enablement doctrines.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing additional defensive options even when the primary invalidity theory fails.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that courts may invalidate claims on enablement grounds even when indefiniteness challenges fail, broadening the range of validity attacks that can succeed on appeal.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of VDPP's patent infringement complaint against Volkswagen without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees as an exceptional case under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The case reinforces that filing frivolous patent infringement claims—particularly where related patents have been rejected under § 101—can result in fee-shifting and personal sanctions against attorneys.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong deterrence against frivolous patent suits, as the affirmance of fee awards and attorney sanctions sends a clear signal against baseless infringement claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of fee-shifting and personal sanctions when pursuing infringement claims involving patents related to those previously rejected on eligibility grounds.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day regulatory deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate participation in antidumping duty sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of agency authority. The court found the statute silent on the specific deadline and that Commerce's rule was the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This preserves Commerce's ability to efficiently administer sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers protected by antidumping duty orders benefit from clearer procedural rules, and Commerce's ability to efficiently process sunset reviews is preserved, maintaining trade remedy protections.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic interested parties who miss the 15-day deadline risk losing antidumping duty protections through automatic revocation, even if the underlying dumping would continue.

impacts.caseName: Ridge Corp. v. Kirk NationaLease Co.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted a preliminary injunction barring the defendants from manufacturing, selling, or importing products alleged to infringe an insulated overhead door patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed and remanded the district court's grant of a preliminary injunction in a patent infringement case involving insulated overhead doors. The decision addresses the standards for preliminary injunctive relief in patent cases, including likelihood of success on the merits of infringement claims and related tortious interference claims based on cease-and-desist letters.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from more rigorous scrutiny of preliminary injunction requests, reducing the risk of being enjoined from product sales before a full merits determination.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a higher bar for obtaining preliminary injunctive relief, potentially allowing competitors to continue selling accused products during lengthy patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient analysis when denying a motion for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 after the asserted patent claims were held invalid under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorney fees, holding that the court's order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent on electronic sweepstakes systems where related patent applications had been rejected under § 101 after Alice, raising questions about whether pursuing infringement claims was objectively baseless. The decision reinforces that district courts must provide reasoned explanations when denying fee petitions in exceptional-case determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from enhanced judicial scrutiny of fee petition denials, increasing the likelihood that frivolous patent assertions—particularly where related applications were rejected on eligibility grounds—will result in fee-shifting.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk that pursuing infringement claims involving patents related to § 101-rejected applications will be deemed exceptional, resulting in fee awards to defendants.
